client: I've been really stressed out lately about this family reunion that's coming up next month. Every time I think about it, my heart just starts racing and I get this tight feeling in my chest, mostly because of what happened with my cousin last year and I really don't know how to face that. I'm not even sure talking about it is going to change anything, but I figured I'd give this a shot.
therapist: It sounds like there's a lot weighing on you around this reunion — that physical anxiety response your body is having tells me this situation really matters to you, even if part of you feels uncertain whether talking will help. I really appreciate you taking that step anyway, because that kind of courage in the face of doubt is worth acknowledging. Can you tell me a little more about what happened with your cousin last year, and what feels most daunting about facing them again?
vocal_descriptors: very high pitch, soft-spoken, moderate-paced speech

client: So last year at my uncle's birthday dinner, I got into this really bad argument with my cousin Marcus about some family money stuff — it got pretty heated and I said some things I'm not proud of, and he said some things that really hurt me too. The worst part is that we never really resolved it, we just kind of stopped talking, and now I feel this mix of guilt about my part in it but also still anger about what he said. What I'm most dreading is walking into that reunion and not knowing whether he's going to ignore me, confront me, or if everyone else already knows about it and has taken sides.
therapist: That mix of guilt and lingering hurt makes complete sense — it's actually really common to hold both of those feelings at the same time, and it doesn't mean anything is wrong with you. What strikes me is that so much of your dread seems to be about the uncertainty — not knowing how Marcus will act or what others think — which your mind might be filling in with worst-case scenarios. What does your gut tell you is the most likely way things will actually unfold when you walk in?
vocal_descriptors: very high pitch, soft-spoken, fast speech

client: Honestly, my gut says it'll probably be this really awkward avoidance thing where Marcus and I just kind of orbit around each other the whole day without actually talking, which almost sounds like a relief but also sounds exhausting and humiliating. But then I also have this nagging fear that he might actually say something in front of everyone, and that thought just spirals into this whole scene in my head where I'm standing there looking like the bad guy. I guess I do see what you mean about worst-case scenarios, but it's hard to just dismiss that fear when it feels so real.
therapist: You're absolutely right that we're not trying to dismiss that fear — it's real and it deserves to be taken seriously, not just pushed aside. I'm noticing you're speaking quite quickly, and I wonder if even just talking through this is stirring up some of that anxious energy, so it might help to take a breath as we slow this down together. If that "public confrontation" scenario did happen, what's the story you're most afraid people would walk away believing about you?
vocal_descriptors: very high pitch, soft-spoken, very rapid speech

client: I think the story I'm most afraid of is that people would see me as the selfish, greedy one who caused all the drama over money — like I'm the villain in the family narrative. That fear feels really tied into this guilt I already carry, because honestly part of me wonders if that's actually true, if I really was the one who handled it badly. It's hard to even say that out loud because I don't fully believe it, but I also can't completely shake it.
therapist: The fact that you can hold both of those things at once — "I don't fully believe I'm the villain, but I can't completely shake it either" — is actually a really important and honest place to be, and it takes courage to say that out loud. In CBT we'd call that a core fear worth examining: not just "what will others think," but "what if their judgment confirms something I already secretly fear about myself." Can we gently look at what actual evidence you have — both for and against — the idea that you were truly the one who handled it badly?
vocal_descriptors: very high pitch, moderate volume, very rapid speech

client: I can try to look at the evidence, but I'm a little worried that I'm not the most objective person to do that exercise — like, my guilt might make me stack the deck against myself, or my defensiveness might make me minimize what I actually did wrong. On the "against" side, I do know that Marcus said some genuinely cruel things about my character that went way beyond the money disagreement, and I remember feeling like I was responding to being attacked rather than just starting something. But on the "for" side, I did raise my voice first and I brought up some old grievances that probably weren't relevant, so I can't pretend I was totally innocent either.
therapist: What you just did is actually remarkably balanced — you named real evidence on both sides without collapsing into either full self-blame or full defensiveness, and that's genuinely hard to do. Your worry about not being objective is itself a sign of good faith, not a reason to distrust yourself entirely. What if the most honest conclusion here is that this was a two-person argument where both of you contributed, rather than a story that needs one clear villain?
vocal_descriptors: very high pitch, moderate volume, fast speech

client: That framing actually does feel more accurate when I hear you say it out loud, and there's a small part of me that feels a little lighter just acknowledging it wasn't entirely my fault. But I guess my worry is that even if I believe that in this room right now, when I'm actually standing in front of Marcus or my aunt or whoever, that whole balanced perspective is just going to evaporate and I'll either freeze up or go back to feeling like the guilty one. It's like I can see the logic of it but I don't trust myself to hold onto it under pressure.
therapist: That gap between "I can see it clearly now" and "I trust myself to hold it under pressure" is one of the most common and frustrating parts of this work, and you're naming it really honestly. The good news is that this balanced perspective isn't something you either have or lose — it's something we can actually practice and reinforce so it becomes more accessible to you in those high-pressure moments, not just here. Would it help to think together about what a small, concrete thing might look like that you could do before or during the reunion to anchor yourself back to this clearer view when the anxiety starts pulling you away from it?
vocal_descriptors: very high pitch, moderate volume, fast speech

client: I'm open to trying something concrete, but I'm a little skeptical about things like breathing exercises or writing affirmations on a notecard, because in my experience when I'm actually anxious those kinds of things feel kind of silly and I end up not doing them. I guess what I'm wondering is whether there's something more natural or less obvious that I could actually see myself using in the moment without feeling self-conscious about it. What would that even look like?
therapist: Your skepticism is actually really useful information — the best coping strategy is one you'll genuinely use, not one that feels performative or awkward in the moment. Something more natural might look like having a pre-planned "exit ramp" — a simple, believable reason to step away for a few minutes if you feel overwhelmed, like grabbing a drink or checking on something, just enough space to reconnect with yourself without anyone noticing. Would something like that feel more like something you could actually see yourself reaching for?
vocal_descriptors: very high pitch, moderate volume, moderate-paced speech

client: Yeah, that actually does sound more like something I could use — it's low-key enough that I wouldn't feel like I'm making a big production out of managing my anxiety in front of everyone. I think the harder part for me is what I do with those few minutes alone, because usually when I step away from a stressful situation my brain just keeps replaying everything and I end up more wound up than before. So I guess I'm wondering if there's something specific I could actually do in that moment to help myself reset, rather than just marinating in the anxiety somewhere quieter.
therapist: That tendency to replay everything when you step away is really common — your brain is trying to problem-solve, but it ends up feeding the anxiety instead of interrupting it. One thing that can work in those moments is giving your mind something very simple and concrete to focus on — not a mantra, but something almost boringly physical, like noticing five things you can see or feel around you, just enough to interrupt the replay loop without requiring much effort. It's less about "calming down" and more about giving your brain a brief off-ramp from the spiral — does that feel like something that might actually fit?
vocal_descriptors: very high pitch, soft-spoken, very rapid speech

client: I think I could actually try that, and I like that you framed it as "boringly physical" because it takes the pressure off of it needing to feel meaningful or therapeutic in the moment. My only hesitation is that I've heard of grounding techniques before and I always assumed they were for people having full panic attacks, not just someone feeling socially anxious and guilty at a family party. But I guess if it's just quietly noticing what's around me, nobody would even know I'm doing it, which makes it feel a lot less weird.
therapist: You're exactly right that grounding isn't just for panic attacks — it's really just a way of interrupting any moment where your mind is running faster than you need it to, which sounds very much like what happens for you at these gatherings. I do notice that even as you're talking through this and finding things that feel workable, there's something in your voice that sounds like it's still carrying a lot of weight — like part of you is still bracing for something. Is there something about the reunion that we haven't quite touched on yet that still feels unresolved for you?
vocal_descriptors: very high pitch, moderate volume, fast speech

client: Yeah, I think there is something I haven't said yet, which is that beyond Marcus, I'm also dreading facing the rest of the family because I've been pretty absent this past year — I kind of withdrew after the argument because I felt so ashamed and I didn't want to deal with anyone's questions or opinions about what happened. So now I'm walking into this reunion carrying not just the guilt about the fight, but also this feeling that I've let people down by disappearing, and I don't know how to explain a whole year of distance in a casual conversation over potato salad. It's like there are two separate things I have to face, and I'm not sure I have enough in me to handle both on the same day.
therapist: What you just shared feels like the real heart of it — the shame that kept you away has quietly grown into a second weight you're now carrying into the same room, and that's a lot for one day. I want to gently reflect that even as you're describing feeling like you don't have enough in you, you're speaking with a lot of energy and clarity about it, which makes me wonder if part of you has been waiting to finally put this into words. Can we sit with this for a moment — because I'm curious whether the story you're telling yourself about "letting people down" is one your family has actually confirmed, or one that shame has been writing for you this past year?
vocal_descriptors: very high pitch, loud, very rapid speech
